newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebel Maskhadov set for Chechen poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Maskhadov set for Chechen poll victory.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who forced Russian troops out of Chechnya with a combination of guerrilla warfare and shrewd diplomacy, appeared certain of a clear victory on Tuesday in the region's presidential polls.

The likely result, backed by a hefty turnout in Monday's vote, will lend weight to the mainly Moslem region's demands for secession from Russia. But Moscow has strong cards to play in negotiations with tiny landlocked Chechnya, which is badly short of cash to rebuild an economy devastated by the war.
At Maskhadov's headquarters in the largely ruined capital, Grozny, camouflage-clad guerrillas with rifles slung over their shoulders hugged each other as women laughed and celebrated.
"Preliminary figures allow us to say that Aslan Maskhadov has become president of Chechnya," said Maskhadov's spokesman Mayerbek Vachagayev, raising a fist in a victory salute.

Concrete results are not expected until late afternoon but electoral officials said partial counts showed Maskhadov would clear the 50 percent of votes needed to avoid a second ballot. Hardline guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev was second, they said.
Across town at Basayev's headquarters among the shell-blasted apartment blocks of Minutka roundabout the mood was sombre. Aides conceded Maskhadov was well ahead in the count.

A Maskhadov victory may be some comfort to Moscow after the humiliation of losing a 21-month war to his tiny guerrilla army. Basayev would be a nightmare for the Kremlin, which wants him for "terrorism".
Russian leaders learned to negotiate with Maskhadov, a soft-spoken ex-Soviet colonel, over the past year.
But he too has sworn to turn de facto autonomy into full sovereignty, something Moscow has flatly rejected and insisted on leaving out of the peace deal signed by Maskhadov last autumn.
"Now Russia will be sitting at the negotiating table with a democratically elected president," Maskhadov's vice-presidential running mate, Vakha Arsanov, told Reuters.

"Despite our...difficulties...we managed to hold truly universal, democratic elections. This should convince the world that the Chechen people have defvended, are defending, and will defend their independence will all the means at their disposal," said acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev as he acknowledged defeat.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said President Boris Yeltsin had expressed satisfaction that the polls took place.
Clearly worried about foreign interference, especially from its southern Moslem neighbours, Russia has threatened to sever relations with any nation that recognises Chechen sovereignty.
Maskhadov, whose aides said had 58 percent of the early count to 30 percent for Basayev, wants "reparations" for the war launched by Moscow, in which tens of thousands of people died.
Russia has promised cash for rebuilding, notably for Chechnya's oil refineries. Those funds will be a vital bargaining chip.
Outside observers have said they were impressed by the smoothness of the voting and an absence of major violations.
There were no reports of violence in a land awash with guns. Maskhadov, 45, says he will work with all the guerrilla leaders to avoid Chechnya sliding into Afghan-style anarchy.
Basayev, however, has accused his military chief of filling his political staff with "criminals".

In Moscow, Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia, called a meeting of his top-level Consultative Council to discuss the results of the poll on Tuesday. The president, not seen in public since January 6, spent three hours in the Kremlin on Tuesday, his spokesman said.
Yeltsin admits that sending troops to crush the Chechen rebels in 1994 was one of his biggest mistakes. It could yet haunt him into a second term overshadowed by illness.
Chechens turned out in large, good-humoured crowds for Monday's vote. Electoral officials said about 70 percent of the half-million electorate may have cast ballots.
People in Grozny voiced mixed emotions over the prospect of Maskhadov as leader.
"I think that today Maskhadov is the best man to stabilise the situation in Chechnya," said one young man.
"Now they (Russia) will have to recognise us. We're people too, like Portugal, Holland. We're not monkeys," said another. "With Maskhadov as president everything will be OK."
But another armed man, with the black beard of a Moslem guerrilla, said: "He may be a soldier, but he's weak. The people who voted for Maskhadov are opposed to independence."
